claims.text: The identity of X (Si, Mn, or Al) governs formation and persistence of a stable protective oxide on CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
X governs oxidation behavior by controlling lattice coherence or misfit at the metal/oxide interface.
Si incorporation minimizes metal/oxide lattice misfit in CrFeCoNiX.
Si promotes a coherent oxide scale with reduced oxygen diffusion.
Mn or Al increases interfacial strain and produces brittle oxides prone to cracking and spallation.
The comparison will vary X among Si, Mn, and Al while holding the base composition and processing constant.
The proposed materials are CrFeCoNiX alloys in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
The hypothesis applies in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C over service-relevant durations.
Metal/oxide lattice misfit determines interfacial strain.
Metal/oxide lattice coherence or misfit affects oxygen diffusivity.
X changes the lattice parameters of the CrFeCoNiX substrate.
Reduced lattice misfit produces a coherent, slow-growing oxide because oxygen diffusion is restricted.
Increased lattice mismatch generates interfacial strain that causes oxide cracking or spallation under thermal stress.
CrFeCoNiSi will form a persistent, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide during high-temperature exposure.
CrFeCoNiMn will form an oxide scale that cracks or spalls because of increased interfacial mismatch and faster oxygen ingress.
CrFeCoNiAl will form an oxide scale that cracks or spalls because of increased interfacial mismatch and faster oxygen ingress.
A CrFeCoNiMn composition is known to exhibit unstable oxide formation and can serve as the baseline.
Compact chromia, alumina, and silica layers can act as diffusion barriers against further oxidation in Cr-, Al-, or Si-containing alloys.
A refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 high-entropy alloy exhibited severe oxidation and specimen disintegration at 900 °C after 50 hours.
